cards.title: Schema-First SDL, Types, Queries, Mutations & Subscriptions
cards.question: Explain Schema-First SDL, Types, Queries, Mutations & Subscriptions
cards.answer_30s: GraphQL exposes a strongly-typed Schema Definition Language (SDL) over a single endpoint: Queries read data, Mutations write data (executed sequentially at top level), and Subscriptions push real-time events over WebSockets/SSE.

code.body:
type Query { user(id: ID!): User }
type Mutation { createPost(input: PostInput!): Post! }

cards.typical_use: Unifying mobile, web, and BFF clients without over-fetching or under-fetching.
pitfalls: Always wrap mutation arguments in a single `input` object type for cleaner backwards-compatible evolution.

cards.title: The N+1 Problem & DataLoader Batching
cards.question: Explain The N+1 Problem & DataLoader Batching
cards.answer_30s: Because nested field resolvers execute per parent item, fetching 50 posts and each post's `author` fires 1 + 50 DB queries. DataLoader batches all keys requested within a single event-loop tick into one `WHERE id IN (...)` query and deduplicates via per-request caching.

code.body:
const userLoader = new DataLoader(ids => db.users.findManyByIds(ids));
// Crucial: instantiate a fresh DataLoader per HTTP request!

cards.typical_use: Eliminating 50x DB latency amplification in GraphQL APIs.
pitfalls: Never share a DataLoader instance globally across requests—that leaks cached user data between requests!

cards.title: Cursor-Based Pagination (Relay Connections)
cards.question: Explain Cursor-Based Pagination (Relay Connections)
cards.answer_30s: Relay-style Connections (`edges { node, cursor }`, `pageInfo { hasNextPage, endCursor }`) provide stable cursor pagination that doesn't drift when new items are inserted, unlike offset pagination.

code.body: query { posts(first: 20, after: "cursor123") { edges { node { id title } } pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor } } }

pitfalls: Encode cursors opaquely (Base64) so clients don't couple to internal DB column formats.

cards.title: Query Depth Limiting, Complexity Analysis & Introspection
cards.question: Explain Query Depth Limiting, Complexity Analysis & Introspection
cards.answer_30s: Malicious clients can craft deeply nested cyclic queries (`user { friends { friends { ... } } }`) to DoS servers. Enforce max query depth, weighted query complexity limits, persisted queries (APQ/allowlists), and disable introspection in production.

code.body: // Enforce maxDepth: 7 and maxComplexity: 500 in validationRules

cards.typical_use: Hardening public GraphQL endpoints against DoS.
pitfalls: Also put timeouts and rate limiting at the gateway/cost layer rather than simple request-count limits.

cards.title: GraphQL Caching & Persisted Queries
cards.question: Explain GraphQL Caching & Persisted Queries
cards.answer_30s: Because GraphQL typically uses POST `/graphql`, standard HTTP CDN caching doesn't work out of the box. Solve this with Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) sent as GET with a query hash, normalized client caches (Apollo/Relay using `id`), and server-side DataLoader/Redis caching.
cards.typical_use: Enabling CDN edge caching and shrinking mobile upload bandwidth.
pitfalls: Persisted query allowlists also block arbitrary ad-hoc queries in production.

cards.title: GraphQL Federation & Schema Stitching
cards.question: Explain GraphQL Federation & Schema Stitching
cards.answer_30s: Apollo Federation lets independent microservice teams own separate subgraphs (`users`, `orders`, `billing`) composed into a single supergraph gateway using `@key` entity references.

code.body: type User @key(fields: "id") { id: ID! name: String! }

cards.typical_use: Scaling GraphQL across dozens of backend teams.
pitfalls: Keep federation gateways focused on composition and auth; avoid putting heavy business logic in the router.

cards.title: Q: GraphQL vs REST vs gRPC — when do you choose each?
cards.question: Q: GraphQL vs REST vs gRPC — when do you choose each?
cards.answer_30s: A: Use REST for simple public APIs, resource caching, and file uploads. Use GraphQL when multiple clients (mobile/web) need flexible, nested data shapes from aggregated sources without over-fetching. Use gRPC for high-throughput, low-latency internal service-to-service RPC with strict Protobuf contracts.

code.body: // External BFF -> GraphQL | Public CRUD -> REST | Internal microservices -> gRPC

pitfalls: Acknowledge GraphQL's added complexity (caching, N+1, rate limiting) rather than pitching it as a silver bullet.

cards.title: Q: How does GraphQL handle errors vs HTTP status codes?
cards.question: Q: How does GraphQL handle errors vs HTTP status codes?
cards.answer_30s: A: GraphQL typically returns `200 OK` with `{ data: ..., errors: [...] }` for partial failures so healthy fields still render. For critical domain errors, senior teams model typed union results in the schema (e.g. `CreateOrderResult = Order | OutOfStockError`) alongside HTTP 401/429 at the gateway.
cards.typical_use: Designing ergonomic error contracts in GraphQL.
pitfalls: Modeling expected business errors as GraphQL union types makes client handling type-safe.

cards.title: Q: How do you handle authentication and field-level authorization in GraphQL?
cards.question: Q: How do you handle authentication and field-level authorization in GraphQL?
cards.answer_30s: A: Authenticate the token once in HTTP middleware and attach `currentUser` to the GraphQL `context`. Enforce coarse-grained checks in resolvers/directives (`@auth(requires: ADMIN)`) or inside the underlying service layer so business rules aren't duplicated.

code.body: // Always pass context.user down to service/domain authorization

pitfalls: Enforcing auth in the service layer ensures REST, GraphQL, and background jobs share the same security rules.

cards.title: Q: Why must DataLoader be created per-request rather than globally?
cards.question: Q: Why must DataLoader be created per-request rather than globally?
cards.answer_30s: A: DataLoader caches loaded results in memory by key. A global DataLoader would serve stale data forever, grow unboundedly into an OOM leak, and leak private records across different users' requests.

code.body: // Create loaders inside context factory: context: ({ req }) => ({ loaders: createLoaders() })

cards.typical_use: Critical DataLoader gotcha tested in almost every GraphQL interview.
pitfalls: Pair per-request DataLoader with Redis for cross-request caching if needed.

cards.title: Q: How do you handle file uploads in GraphQL?
cards.question: Q: How do you handle file uploads in GraphQL?
cards.answer_30s: A: Avoid streaming large binaries through GraphQL multipart requests. Instead, use a GraphQL mutation `createUploadUrl` to return a short-lived S3 Presigned URL, let the client upload directly to object storage, and pass the resulting file key to a follow-up mutation.
cards.typical_use: Clean architecture for media-heavy GraphQL apps.
pitfalls: Presigned URLs keep GraphQL servers fast and stateless.

cards.title: Q: How do you evolve a GraphQL schema without breaking old mobile clients?
cards.question: Q: How do you evolve a GraphQL schema without breaking old mobile clients?
cards.answer_30s: A: GraphQL avoids `/v1`/`/v2` URL versioning. Instead, add new fields/types additively, mark old fields `@deprecated(reason: "Use fullName")`, monitor field usage telemetry, and remove deprecated fields only after old client versions drop to zero.
pitfalls: Never make a nullable field non-nullable or remove an enum value without checking client telemetry.
